ex: HSP/IGAV is self-limiting; steroids are reserved for significant GI or renal disease.

q: A 12-year-old girl with short stature and absent pubertal development has webbed neck and a 45,X karyotype. Which cardiac defect is most characteristic of this syndrome?
ex: Coarctation of aorta is the characteristic cardiac lesion of Turner syndrome.

q: A 6-year-old boy fatigues on playing football and has calf cramps; resting creatine kinase is elevated and ischemic exercise fails to raise lactate. Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: McArdle disease (GSD V): muscle phosphorylase deficiency with flat lactate response.

q: A 10-month-old with developmental regression and a cherry-red macula has no organomegaly. Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: Tay-Sachs: hexosaminidase A deficiency; cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly.

q: A 7-year-old has pancytopenia; marrow shows Gaucher cells with a crumpled paper cytoplasm. Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: Gaucher disease: glucocerebrosidase (beta-glucosidase) deficiency with Gaucher cells and organomegaly.

q: A 6-week-old infant with progressive hypotonia, macroglossia, hepatomegaly and cardiomegaly on chest film; ECHO shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which enzyme is deficient?
ex: Pompe disease (GSD II): acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency causing cardiomegaly and floppy baby picture.

q: A 4-month-old of an HIV-positive mother has recurrent diarrhea and failure to thrive. Which test establishes infant HIV infection earliest?
ex: Maternal antibodies cross placenta, so virologic testing (DNA/RNA PCR) is used in the first 18 months.

q: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent pneumonia, sinusitis and skin boils since infancy; IgG levels are normal. Which defect best explains the picture?
ex: CGD: NADPH oxidase defect causing catalase-positive staphylococcal abscesses; confirm by DHR/NBT test.

q: A 7-year-old develops abdominal pain, vomiting, oliguria and periorbital edema after induction chemotherapy for ALL; uric acid 12 mg/dL and potassium 6.5 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Aggressive IV hydration with allopurinol and treat hyperkalemia
ex: Tumor lysis syndrome: hyperuricemia-hyperkalemia-hyperphosphatemia; hydration, allopurinol and K+ management first.

q: A 2-year-old with fever, stridor and barking cough; neck film shows the steeple sign. Which organism is typical?
ex: Croup/laryngotracheobronchitis is viral, classically parainfluenza; steeple sign on AP neck film.

q: A 6-week-old with persistent hypoglycemia requiring a glucose infusion rate over 15 mg/kg/min, with inappropriately low ketones during hypoglycemia. Which is the most likely cause?
ex: Persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy: high GIR need plus hypoketotic hypoglycemia; treat with diazoxide.

q: A 4-week-old has recurrent non-bilious projectile vomiting. X-ray shows a single gastric air bubble and no gas beyond the stomach. Which is the next investigation of choice?
ex: USG shows elongated pyloric canal (target/antral nipple sign); contrast studies are avoided where USG available.

q: A 2-day-old term neonate fails to pass meconium, has abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Barium enema reveals a narrow distal segment with a transitional zone. Which cell type is absent in the narrow segment?
o: Ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus
ex: Hirschsprung disease: aganglionosis of Auerbach and Meissner plexuses.

q: A 6-week-old with vomiting has an X-ray showing a single bubble. Which obstruction does this represent?
ex: Single gastric bubble = gastric outlet obstruction, classically pyloric stenosis.

q: A 2-week-old has projectile vomiting and weight loss; ultrasound shows a target sign at the pylorus. What is the definitive treatment?
ex: Correct alkalosis first, then Ramstedt pyloromyotomy for IHPS.

q: A 1-day-old neonate has not voided since birth; bladder is not palpable. Which is the next step?
o: Reassure and observe 24 hours with continued breastfeeding
ex: >97% of term babies void by 24 h; observation and feeding is standard first step.

q: A 6-week-old with persistent jaundice, umbilical hernia and hypotonia has TSH 130 mIU/L and low T4. Thyroid USG shows a eutopic gland. What is the next investigation?
ex: Eutopic gland + high TSH suggests dyshormonogenesis; nuclear scan assesses uptake.

q: A newborn at 38 weeks has persistent pulmonary hypertension with severe hypoxemia. Which is the first-line pulmonary vasodilator in term neonates?
ex: iNO is the specific pulmonary vasodilator used for PPHN with good response.

q: A term neonate develops grunting, intercostal retractions and cyanosis at 4 hours of age; chest film shows a leftward mediastinal shift with a right-sided opaque hemithorax. What is the diagnosis?
ex: Bowel loops in the right chest shift the mediastinum; CDH causes persistent pulmonary hypertension.

q: A 2-week-old infant has choking with feeds, excessive drooling and recurrent pneumonia. Which is the first investigation?
o: Passage of a nasogastric tube to check resistance at 10-12 cm
ex: Resistance to NG tube passage ~10-12 cm from the gums suggests esophageal atresia; confirmed by X-ray.

q: A 4-year-old with unsteady gait, upgoing plantar and MRI showing periventricular white matter changes; he has consanguineous parents. Which enzyme is deficient in the most common form?
ex: Metachromatic leukodystrophy: arylsulfatase A deficiency, autosomal recessive.

q: A 5-year-old with recurrent sinopulmonary infections has decreased IgA but normal IgG and IgM. Which condition is associated with this defect?
ex: Selective IgA deficiency associates with celiac disease, sinusitis and anaphylaxis to blood products.

q: A 14-month-old had a GTC seizure lasting 4 minutes with fever 39.2 C, self-resolving with full recovery; CSF is normal. What is the single most important risk factor for recurrence?
o: Age under 12 months at first seizure
ex: Younger age at first febrile seizure (<12 months) carries the highest recurrence risk.

q: A neonate with seizures at 48 hours has hypoglycemia, micropenis and undescended testes. Which hormone replacement is most critical?
ex: Congenital hypopituitarism: cortisol replacement is lifesaving in neonatal hypoglycemia.

q: A 2-month-old infant with eczema and recurrent infections has a neutrophil NBT test showing no formazan reduction. Which pathogen is most characteristic of this disorder?
ex: CGD: catalase-positive organisms, especially S. aureus and Aspergillus, cause abscesses.

q: A 6-month-old infant has severe hypotonia, tongue fasciculations and poor feeding; EMG shows denervation. Which is the most common genetic cause in infancy?
o: Spinal muscular atrophy type I (SMN1 deletion)
ex: SMA type I (Werdnig-Hoffmann): SMN1 deletion, proximal weakness with preserved facial expression.

q: A 9-year-old boy has painless hematuria; renal biopsy shows IgA deposition in the mesangium after an URTI. Which is the most common primary glomerulonephritis in children worldwide?
ex: IgA nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis in children.

q: A newborn at 34 weeks, weight 2.6 kg and born to a 23-year-old mother, develops tachypnea at 2 hours with mild retractions; X-ray shows prominent central pulmonary vascular markings and fluid in the fissures; symptoms resolve in 36 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: TTN: benign course with perihilar streaking and fissural fluid in late preterm/term babies.

q: A 3-day-old preterm on CPAP with abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and blood in stools; X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the next step in management?
o: NPO with IV fluids, antibiotics and serial abdominal X-rays
ex: NEC: medical management with bowel rest and antibiotics; surgery only for perforation.

q: A 1-week-old baby with an infected umbilicus and redness spreading over the abdominal wall develops shock. Which organism is the most common cause of neonatal tetanus-like syndrome and omphalitis in this setting?
ex: S. aureus is the commonest cause of omphalitis and newborn skin sepsis.

q: A 6-week-old infant with cough and tachypnea for 3 weeks; X-ray shows hyperinflation with diffuse interstitial infiltrates; CBC shows lymphocytosis with typical smear findings; mother is HIV negative. Which drug is the treatment of choice?
ex: Pertussis: macrolides (azithromycin) are the drugs of choice in infancy.

q: A 2-month-old with fever and lethargy has a bulging fontanelle; CSF shows 800 WBCs (70% polymorphs), glucose 20 mg/dL, protein 120 mg/dL; culture grows Gram-negative rods. What is the most likely pathogen?
ex: After the neonatal period, E. coli and GBS dominate infant meningitis; here E. coli fits the Gram-negative smear.

q: A 6-year-old with hematuria, edema and hypertension 3 weeks after a sore throat has low C3, ASO 400 IU and RBC casts. Which statement is correct about management?
o: Supportive care; steroids are not indicated
ex: Post-streptococcal GN: supportive; C3 returns to normal in 6-8 weeks.

q: A 3-year-old with nephrotic syndrome has a renal biopsy showing minimal change disease. What is the first-line induction therapy?
ex: Minimal change disease responds to corticosteroids in >90% of children.

q: A 7-year-old presents with excessive thirst, polyuria, weight loss and a random glucose of 550 mg/dL with ketones. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: 0.9% saline 10-20 mL/kg over 1 hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/hr
ex: DKA: fluid resuscitation first; no insulin bolus; add dextrose when glucose <250-300 mg/dL.
